Emphasis is placed on self-initiative, the development of skills in teamwork, and the application of a critical, science-based approach to practical nutrition.

clos.text: Analyse the role and importance of nutrients and evaluate how different forms of energy provision affect animals' ability to satisfy their requirements.
Explain the interactions between carbohydrates, proteins and lipids in animal metabolism and predict how imbalances result in dysfunction and inefficiency.

Formulate diets for animals from first principles to match the energy and protein requirements, limiting amino acids, major minerals and vitamins and describe their roles in metabolism at different physiological stages across species

Explain the environmental and seasonal factors that influence feed availability and quality, and explain how pasture assessment and grazing management strategies, can be used to support animal nutrition in extensive production systems.
Identify body composition and use critical thinking to design different feeding strategies across species to address animal health, welfare and production under different scenarios.
Apply critical thinking and an evidence-based approach to animal nutrition and demonstrate skills in data collection, analysis, synthesis, report writing, collaboration and communication skills.

courses.title: Research Methodology for Animal Science 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed STAT1000 Data Skills for Scientists
courses.aim: This course focuses on understanding and application of the scientific method in biological research, and in particular, the animal sciences.

clos.text: Demonstrate effective written, oral and graphical presentation skills
Apply the principles and practices of experimental design in animal science and animal behaviour, including development of scientific hypotheses
Demonstrate the selection and application of appropriate statistical methods to authentic data
Correctly interpret the outcomes of statistical testing
Perform project management in the context of planning a research project through working in small groups

courses.title: Professional Skills in Animal Science 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of ANIM1000 Animal Handling and Husbandry/ANIM1001 Principles of Animal Behaviour, Welfare and Ethics
courses.aim: This course aims to enhance students' understanding of the professional, personal and discipline-specific skills relevant to careers in the animal science industries. Training will be provided in career planning, communication and business skills. Students will be encouraged to apply their research and critical thinking skills, and to integrate and apply knowledge gained across the animal science disciplines, through consideration of current issues facing the animal sciences and the potential impact of these issues on their future careers. Students must have completed 200 hours of work experience placements, and the course will include reflection and assessment of work-place learning experiences.

clos.text: Critically evaluate challenges facing the animal science industries and disciplines, and the potential strategies to address these challenges
Identify skills and capabilities that intersect effectively with the needs of industry in the area of animal science
Demonstrate career planning skills and an understanding of the employability attributes required to develop a career pathway in the area of animal science
Apply reflective practice in relation to workplace learning experiences
Communicate effectively and professionally

courses.title: Animal Breeding and Genetics
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of BIOL1003 Biology 1A: Molecules, Genes and Cells/BIOL1004 Biology 1B: Evolution and Diversity of Organisms
excl: ANIMLSC3045RW Animal Breeding and Genetics III at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed ANIMLSC3045RW Animal Breeding and Genetics III at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: The application of scientific methods to animal breeding has led to major improvements in the output, cost and quality of meat, milk and fibre. In addition, animal breeding plans are important for continued improvement of companion animals and management of endangered species. Topics include an introduction to quantitative genetics, maximising response to selection, crossbreeding, estimation of genetic parameters and breeding values, mode of inheritance, mating systems, fitness and quality traits, animal diversity, development of breeding programs, use of biotechnology in breeding programs including gene mapping and parentage testing. Examples will be drawn from Australia's livestock industries as well as wildlife and companion animals.

clos.text: Describe the tools available to maximise response to genetic selection in a variety of animal species
Describe inbreeding and crossbreeding effects related to production and conservation of species
Describe complex inheritance
Assess animal phenotypes and make selection decisions based on that structure
Design a breeding program

courses.title: Intensive Animal Production Science 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed ANIM1000 Animal Handling and Husbandry OR must have completed AGRI1000 Agricultural Production
excl: ANIMLSC3047RW Intensive Animal Production Science III at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed ANIMLSC3047RW Intensive Animal Production Science III at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: Intensive Animal Production Science deals with the application of science to intensive animal production systems. Production systems include pigs, poultry and aquaculture. The management of these systems are discussed in detail, covering all aspects of production, including genetics and breeding, animal nutrition and growth performance, environmental and welfare requirements, health status, reproductive efficiency and product (meat and egg) quality. This course will also consider the advantages and disadvantages of various modern production systems, including biosecurity measures, welfare considerations, economic factors, the demand for product consistency, food safety issues, and other consumer expectations.

clos.text: Describe the science underlying the genetics, reproduction, nutrition, environment and health of pigs, poultry and aquaculture species
Demonstrate how factors such as genetics, environment, nutrition and health can be manipulated to improve the efficiency of an intensive production enterprise
Discuss the importance and complexity of biosecurity measures in intensive production enterprises
Integrate and assess individual management strategies to design a complete intensive production enterprise that can be analysed
Discuss the impact of contemporary issues (e.g. animal welfare, antibiotic use and environmental) and application of new technologies in intensive production enterprises

courses.title: Laboratory Animal Science 3
excl: ANIMLSC3100RW Laboratory Animal Science III at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed ANIMLSC3100RW Laboratory Animal Science III at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: This course aims to instil the major principles of the study of laboratory animals and their utilisation for teaching, research and commercial purposes. This will include developing a scientific understanding of the applications and limitations of various laboratory animal species in addition to practical experience in animal handling and other procedures. Topics will include animal handling, breeding, feeding, maintenance, minor interceptions and minor surgical procedures. Students will be involved with a research project in which relevant aspects of laboratory animal science will be undertaken. Species studied will include mice, rats, guinea pigs and rabbits. The student will become familiar with processes associated with induction of gastrointestinal diseases and disorders in rats and mice which affect humans. These disorders could include chemotherapy-induced mucositis, gastric ulceration and inflammatory bowel disease. Students will also be exposed to the ways in which the animal models can be utilised, for example, in the testing of new treatment modalities. The course will incorporate two field trips to facilities associated with laboratory animal use.

clos.text: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the scientific importance and physical requirements associated with aspects of laboratory animal handling, breeding, feed, maintenance, and minor surgical procedures
Describe the processes associated with induction of gastrointestinal diseases and disorders which affect humans through the use of animal models in laboratory animal species
Locate, analyse and evaluate information from a variety of sources
Demonstrate the ability to handle a variety of laboratory animal species, including the collection of material from these specimens
Demonstrate the ability to work as part of a team through the collation and presentation of information in small team-based projects

courses.title: Animals and the Law
excl: ANIMLSC3250RW Animals and the Law at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed ANIMLSC3250RW Animals and the Law at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: This course will look at the ethics and jurisprudence on the way humans think of and treat animals, the history and present status of animals as property, and the statutory and case law in which non-humans play a part. The course will involve visits to different animal enterprises in order to assess how the law works in practice and the effectiveness of enforcement in these real life situations.

clos.text: Demonstrate a knowledge of the basic framework of animal-related legislation in Australia
Show how the law is applied to animals and animal-based enterprises
Interpret and apply legislation to animal-based enterprises
Show an understanding of the difficulties in creating legislation relevant to animals and animal-based enterprises

courses.title: Parasitology III
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL1003 Biology 1A: Molecules, Genes and Cells OR must have completed BIOL1004 Biology 1B: Evolution and Diversity of Organisms OR must have completed VETS1000 Foundations of Science for Veterinary Technologists
excl: ANIMLSC3515RW Parasitology III at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed VETS3004 Veterinary Parasitology OR must not have completed ANIMLSC3515RW Parasitology III at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: This course will cover the scientific discipline of parasitology and the relationship between parasites and disease at the tissue and animal level in various animal hosts and body systems. The course will provide students with the theoretical and practical skills required in parasitology, including the diagnosis, control and treatment of common parasite diseases, including zoonosis.

clos.text: Integrate knowledge and the terminology, basic principles and application of parasitology
Demonstrate competency in the core components of diagnostic parasitology
Demonstrate competency in practical laboratory skills
Utilise knowledge in the application of parasite control and treatment methodologies

courses.title: Ecology and Management of Vertebrate Pests 3
courses.exclText: must not have completed all of ANIMLSC3019RW Ecology and Management of Vertebrate Pests III at the University of Adelaide/HBIO3014 Ecology and Management of Vertebrate Pests III
courses.aim: This course strongly emphasises the field application of vertebrate pest control techniques and provides the theoretical bases for these techniques. Topics covered are the biology and ecology of vertebrate pests; the damage caused by pest animals; the legislative and administrative aspects of vertebrate pest control; district organisations; extension; vertebrate pest control practice. Note: There is a 5 day field trip as a compulsory component of this course.

clos.text: Describe the biological parameters that underpin the application of control techniques to pest populations
Apply pest control techniques
Describe the environmental and agricultural imperatives for pest control
Recognise the welfare implications of pest control

courses.title: Advanced Applications in Animal Behaviour
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of ANIM1000 Animal Handling and Husbandry/ANIM2013 Foundations in Animal Behaviour 2/ANIM3004 Research Methodology for Animal Science 3
courses.aim: The course provides a combination of course work and industry placement. The aim of the course is for the students to apply their animal behaviour discipline knowledge and research skills, as well as develop industry experience. In addition to expert subject knowledge, the course supports students in developing and improving critical thinking and problem-solving skills using scientific methods as well as developing communication skills.

clos.text: Design a research project drawing on experimental design principles and animal behaviour knowledge.
Apply data collection and analysis skills to conduct a research project investigating an animal behaviour topic.
Communicate research findings, e.g. through written report, in line current professional standards.
Critically reflect on and evaluate the animal behaviour workplace experience and their contribution to future employment.
Evaluate personal abilities, knowledge and skills and their contribution to employability in the area of animal behaviour.

courses.title: Biochemistry 3 Molecular and Structural Biology
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of BIOL2015 Biochemistry 2: Metabolism/BIOL2017 Biochemistry 2: Molecular and Cellular Biology
courses.exclText: must not have completed BIOL3021 Molecular and Structural Biology III
courses.aim: The course aims to provide a molecular level understanding of cellular processes, under two principal themes. (1) Protein Structure and Function, where topics include structure and function of different classes of proteins, protein folding, targeted protein degradation, molecular interactions, recognition and allostery. (2) Control of Gene Expression where topics include genetic circuits and synthetic biology; chromatin structure and its remodelling during transcription; the recruitment and assembly of transcription factors and the RNA polymerase complex on a gene promoter; artificially manipulating gene expression with the use of “designer genes” and synthetic transcription factors; eukaryote mRNA synthesis, processing, modification, stability and translation.

clos.text: CLO1: Understand aspects of protein structure and function, including protein folding, degradation, molecular interactions and recognition, allostery and the development of new therapies.

CLO2: Describe the control of gene expression, including design of genetic circuits, an understanding of chromatin structure and remodelling, gene promoter assembly, eukaryotic mRNA synthesis, processing and translation.
CLO3: Understand key experimental processes and apply this knowledge to solve specific biochemical problems.
CLO4: Find, read, interpret and critically analyse relevant scientific literature.
CLO5: Demonstrate the ability to work in teams and effectively communicate scientific outcomes.

courses.title: Biochemistry 3 Molecular Basis of Cancer
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of BIOL2015 Biochemistry 2: Metabolism/BIOL2017 Biochemistry 2: Molecular and Cellular Biology
courses.aim: This course covers major conceptual and technical advances underpinning the molecular basis of cancer and explores how this knowledge is applied to understand, diagnose and treat cancer. Topics are focused on the hallmarks of cancer, encompassing contributions of both tumour cells and the non-tumour microenvironment. Specific examples are included of current diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for cancer treatment.

clos.text: Analyse the molecular basis of the initiation and progression of cancer
Evaluate molecular approaches used in cancer diagnosis, prognosis and treatment
Design experimental strategies to investigate questions in cancer biology
Critically evaluate scientific literature related to the molecular basis of cancer
Communicate scientific concepts effectively in teams and with professional stakeholders
Reflect and discuss how the field of cancer biology has progressed and your thinking about cancer research has changed

courses.title: Genetics 3A: Evolutionary Genetics and Epigenetics
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of BIOL2005 Genetics 2A: Introduction to Genetic Analysis/BIOL2006 Genetics 2B: Applications of Genetic Analysis
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of how evolutionary forces shape the genomes and how gene expression can be regulated epigenetically. By exploring the interplay between DNA variation, gene expression, and epigenetic modifications students will gain insights into how organisms adapt over time and the broader implications for human health and species conservation. This course expands from the foundation laid in Genetics 2A and 2B and presents cutting edge research topics in molecular evolution and epigenetics.

clos.text: Critically evaluate the origin, structure, function, and evolution of genomes and chromosomes within molecular and evolutionary genetics frameworks.
Apply advanced evolutionary genetic concepts to explain the major evolutionary transitions in the history of life.
Evaluate primary scientific literature in epigenetics, cytogenetics and evolutionary genetics.
Integrate and apply advanced current genetic and evolutionary concepts to exercises, problem-solving activities, and scientific discussions.

courses.title: Molecular and Biomedical Sciences Practical 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL2900 Molecular and Biomedical Science Practical 2
courses.aim: Students will build advanced laboratory skills for Molecular and Biomedical Science majors (Genetics, Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology) which includes a group research project or individual research laboratory placement.

clos.text: Demonstrate hands-on practical experimental skills and techniques frequently used in molecular and biomedical research
Demonstrate essential skills in experimental design, results, analysis and problem solving
Demonstrate appropriate application of computer-based tools to investigate molecular and biomedical research questions
Work effectively in small teams and communicate outcomes to a larger group of colleagues
Demonstrate safe laboratory practise

courses.title: Infection and Immunity 3A
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL2021 Microbiology 2
courses.aim: This advanced course examines the molecular basis of host-pathogen interactions for bacterial and parasitic infections of significant global and medical importance. This includes how these interactions contribute to pathogenesis. The importance of vaccines, antimicrobial drugs, the microbiome and tools used to research and identify pathogens will also be discussed. The course structure includes tutorials and workshops which extend skills in exploring and critically assessing the scientific literature. This course will provide the theoretical basis for Microbiology and Immunology Practical III.

clos.text: Articulate molecular mechanisms underpinning the growth of bacterial and parasitic pathogens, and how they interact with the host and their environments
Explain how bacterial and parasitic pathogens respond to and overcome control measures
Critically evaluate contemporary experimental techniques and strategies used to investigate the biological mechanisms underpinning bacterial and parasitic pathology and survival
Review, summarise and discuss research papers relevant to bacterial and parasitic infections of global importance
Work collegially in small teams to understand scientific problems and processes, and communicate these effectively to staff and peers
Use Gen-AI effectively and responsibly to assist in understanding theoretical concepts, and to construct a framework for an extended written piece

courses.title: Infection and Immunity 3B
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL2008 Immunology and Virology 2
courses.aim: This course aims to provide students with advanced understanding of the immune system in health and disease.

clos.text: Articulate specific cellular and molecular processes involved in the function of the immune system in health and disease
Integrate concepts in immunology and microbial pathogenesis to demonstrate understanding of complex human disease
Explain fundamental concepts of how viruses interact with the host cell, replicate and evade immune responses
Demonstrate understanding of vaccine design and application as it applies to microbial pathogens
Work in small teams and effectively communicate concepts related to recent advances in immunology and viral pathogenesis

courses.title: Biochemistry 3: Practical
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of BIOL2015 Biochemistry 2: Metabolism/BIOL2017 Biochemistry 2: Molecular and Cellular Biology/BIOL2900 Molecular and Biomedical Science Practical 2
courses.aim: This practical course will consolidate the biochemical concepts covered in Level II and Level III Biochemistry lecture courses. The practical exercises will be centred around a real-world research project where the experimental outcome is unknown, giving students an insight into the excitement of discovering new information. Research project themes will align with the major concepts covered in level 3 lectures including cutting edge techniques in recombinant DNA technology, protein expression and purification, synthetic biology or cancer research/drug discovery.

clos.text: Demonstrate hands-on practical experimental skills and techniques frequently used in biomedical research, as it relates to biochemistry
Demonstrate essential skills in experimental design, results, analysis and problem solving
Demonstrate appropriate application of computer-based tools to investigate biochemical research questions
Work effectively in small teams and communicate outcomes with a larger group of colleagues
Demonstrate safe laboratory practise

courses.title: Microbiology and Immunology Practical 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL2900 Molecular and Biomedical Science Practical 2 AND must have completed 1 of BIOL2008 Immunology and Virology 2/BIOL2021 Microbiology 2
courses.aim: This course provides practical skills relevant to microbiology, virology and immunology at an advanced level.

clos.text: Demonstrate hands-on practical experimental skills and techniques frequently used in biomedical research and diagnostic applications.
Critique experimental design, results, analysis and problem solving as it relates to microbiology and immunology.
Demonstrate appropriate application of in silico analysis tools to investigate medically relevant pathogens.
Work effectively in small teams and communicate outcomes using discipline specific terminology with a larger group of colleagues.
Demonstrate safe laboratory practise

courses.title: Research Methods: Ecology, Marine and Wildlife 3
courses.prereq: SCIE2000 AND (BIOL2004 OR BIOL2023 OR BIOL2024 OR BIOL2051)
courses.prereqText: must have completed SCIE2000 Scientific Data: Analysis and Visualisation AND must have completed 1 of BIOL2004 Zoology 2/BIOL2023 Botany 2/BIOL2024 Foundations in Plant Science/BIOL2051 Principles of Ecology 2
courses.aim: This course provides students with vital skills for professional placements and research pathways. Building upon SCIE 2000 (Scientific Data: Analysis and Visualisation), students will apply modern statistical approaches to analyse and interpret real-world datasets from the fields of ecology, marine biology, and wildlife conservation. Using R statistical software, students will employ different data types to answer a range of applied questions, from identifying the drivers of species distributions and population dynamics, to classifying the provenance of seafood and quantifying how environmental gradients shape biological communities.

clos.text: Understand and explain sampling and experimental designs in the ecological and biological sciences.
Apply appropriate statistical techniques to real-world data, evaluate their underlying assumptions, and interpret and communicate results accurately and clearly.
Use R to manipulate and visualise data and to conduct statistical modelling and hypothesis testing.
Critically evaluate and interpret a range of models used to analyse complex patterns and relationships in biological systems.

courses.title: Human Ecology and Global Change
courses.prereqText: must have completed 2 of BIOL2036 Life on Earth A/BIOL2037 Life on Earth B/BIOL2040 Evolution
prereqNotes: 2 of: BIOL2036, BIOL2037, BIOL2040
excl: BIOL3026 Human Ecology and Global Change at the University of South Australia
courses.exclText: must not have completed BIOL3026 Human Ecology and Global Change at the University of South Australia
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to provide students with an understanding of how humans evolved to become the most influential organism on the planet, changing landscapes and climate. Human evolution, the advent of technology and agriculture, building of societies, changes to human nutrition, demographics and disease. Impacts of humans on the planet, focussing on biological systems.

clos.text: Describe the evolution of humans in relation to other primates and the changing evolutionary theories.
Analyse human societial changes and the impact on built environments and global resource use.
Describe how changes to human societies impacted nutrition, and lifespan.
Describe how humans have impacted global climate systems.
Explain how changes to human ecology have in turn impacted lifespan, demographics, and disease, and to make predictions of future impacts.
Analyse human global impacts to current biological settings, including those influencing human health and consider governance policy implications

courses.title: Marine Ecology 3
courses.prereq: (ANIM2002 OR BIOL2004 OR BIOL2023 OR BIOL2051)
courses.prereqText: must have completed 1 of ANIM2002 Comparative Animal Anatomy and Physiology 2/BIOL2004 Zoology 2/BIOL2023 Botany 2/BIOL2051 Principles of Ecology 2
courses.aim: This course develops students’ understanding of foundational marine ecological principles and their application to real-world environmental decision-making. Students examine the processes shaping the distribution and abundance of marine organisms, including natural and anthropogenic drivers, and gain practical experience in field data collection and ecological analysis. An optional field camp during the mid-semester break provides additional hands-on experience with marine ecological survey methods. Through online learning, fieldwork, class discussions and data interpretation, students build skills in scientific inquiry and evidence-based reasoning. These foundations are then applied to a marine management scenario, where students evaluate environmental impacts, design monitoring strategies, and communicate scientific recommendations. The course prepares students to critically assess ecological evidence and contribute to informed, transparent decision-making in marine environmental management.

clos.text: Demonstrate knowledge of key marine ecological concepts governing the distribution, abundance, and interactions of marine organisms, including the influence of natural and anthropogenic drivers.
Design and implement basic marine ecological field surveys using appropriate and ethical field methodologies.
Analyse and interpret ecological datasets to identify patterns, assess environmental change, and draw evidence-based conclusions.
Evaluate potential environmental impacts by applying ecological theory, monitoring frameworks, and evidence-based reasoning.
Communicate scientific findings and recommendations effectively to both specialist and non-specialist audiences through oral presentations and written formats.

courses.title: Molecular Methods in Ecology and Evolution
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL2022 Evolutionary Biology 2
courses.exclText: must not have completed ENV BIOL 3545 (UoA)
courses.aim: This course provides the knowledge and skills to apply molecular data for biodiversity monitoring, conservation, biosecurity and environmental impact assessments. Building on earlier concepts in ecology and evolution, it provides an in-depth exploration of the concepts, molecular approaches and analytical techniques used in these fields. This course is designed to equip students with the necessary knowledge and practical skills for employment in the rapidly expanding field of environmental genomics.

clos.text: Demonstrate theoretical and practical skills in sample collection and molecular data generation and interpretation from animal, plant, microbial and environmental samples
Identify appropriate molecular approaches for a range of ecological and evolutionary applications
Explain the theoretical, practical and ethical limitations and challenges, and importance of incorporating Indigenous perspectives in molecular research.
Interpret molecular data and analyses appropriately and produce scientifically appropriate conclusions and recommendations.
Demonstrate effective scientific communication both orally and in writing following conventions for scientific and industry reporting.
Demonstrate effective time management, project management and team-work and leadership skills.

courses.title: Freshwater Ecology 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed 1 of BIOL2004 Zoology 2/BIOL2023 Botany 2/BIOL2051 Principles of Ecology 2
courses.aim: The course provides theoretical understanding and practical implications of the ecology and restoration of freshwater habitats with a focus on hydrology, nutrient cycles, aquatic biota and food webs. Students will gain a solid foundation in how freshwater ecosystems actually work in Australia, and why so many of them are threatened. This course will build on previous ecology and related course knowledge to distinguish habitats of lakes, wetlands, streams and rivers by varying circulation types, nutrient cycles and food webs. Skills for the identification of algae, zooplankton and water plants as well as for monitoring, assessment and management of drinking water reservoirs, urban and floodplain wetlands, and rivers will be developed during practicals in the laboratory. This course includes a compulsory 5 day field camp at Calperum Station during the mid-semester break.

clos.text: Analyse the structure and functioning of freshwater systems under changing environmental and climatic conditions.
Evaluate habitat requirements, water quality, and ecological processes to inform management and restoration of freshwater systems.
Apply appropriate monitoring, assessment, and modelling methods to evaluate water quality, aquatic biodiversity, and ecosystem integrity.
Design, document, and report ecological investigations using relevant research literature, data, and scientific conventions.
Collaborate effectively to plan, execute, and report applied aquatic ecology investigations.

courses.title: Evolutionary Biology 3 Theory
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL2022 Evolutionary Biology 2 OR must have completed ENVBIOL2501 Evolutionary Biology
prereqNotes: ENVBIOL2501 Evolutionary Biology
courses.exclText: must not have completed ENVBIOL3560
courses.assumed: BIOL2004 - Zoology 2 BIOL2023 - Botany 2 or BIOL2064 - Zoology II BIOL2055 - Botany II
courses.aim: This course aims to build on foundational knowledge of evolutionary biology to provide the advanced concepts and background to accompany practical experience in Level 3. Students will develop advanced theoretical understanding of modern advances in systematics, micro and macro-evolution, palaeontology and palaeobiology. A theme explored in detail throughout the course will be the evolutionary history and contemporary diversity of the Australian biota.

clos.text: Critically evaluate concepts in evolutionary biology
Synthesise processes in evolutionary biology to understand the drivers of biodiversity
Evaluate the role of the fossil record underpinning evolution of Australian biota
Communicate effective evidence-based interpretations of evolutionary concepts to Australian biota

courses.title: Evolutionary Biology 3 Practical
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of BIOL2022 Evolutionary Biology 2/BIOL3035 Evolutionary Biology 3 Theory
courses.exclText: must not have completed ENV BIOL 3590 (UoA)
courses.aim: This course provides advanced practical experience in the research approaches used to address key topics in evolutionary biology and biodiversity conservation.

clos.text: Evaluate cutting-edge practical methodologies that address problems in evolutionary biology and explain the importance of evolutionary studies as a foundation of comparative biology

Design and execute a research project, including statistically sound sampling strategies and the analysis and interpretation of methodologies for the reconstruction and interpretation of phylogenetic and biogeographic patterns and processes
Analyse the importance of the fossil record in evolutionary studies and the role of phylogenetic studies in the wider context of biodiversity and conservation

Present experimental results relating to the Australian biota in a written and oral form that aligns with conventions for scientific reports and discuss scientific matters of current international interest in an informed manner
Demonstrate team-oriented management of projects, especially communication with peers

courses.title: Conservation Biology 3
courses.prereq: (ANIM2002 OR BIOL2004 OR BIOL2023 OR BIOL2051)
courses.prereqText: must have completed 1 of ANIM2002 Comparative Animal Anatomy and Physiology 2/BIOL2004 Zoology 2/BIOL2023 Botany 2/BIOL2051 Principles of Ecology 2
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to utilize conservation biology theory and ecological and evolutionary techniques to address conservation issues for biodiversity at local and global scales, ranging from the gene through to the ecosystem. The course will focus on a variety of biomes in Australia and around the world, covering topics such as the impacts of introduced species, loss of habitat and its degradation, over exploitation, climate change and resultant management strategies. It will also address practical conservation monitoring methods and effective interventions such as reserve design, and social and political factors in decision-making. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to apply their theoretical and applied learnings in conservation to the development of management plans for preventing biodiversity loss, and the services it provides to nature and people. This course aligns with a degree in biology by addressing drivers of biodiversity and their maintenance, and delivers the practical skills, research techniques and ethical awareness needed to assist with careers in conservation management.

clos.text: Effectively use ecological, biological, sociological, legislative, and ethical perspectives to inform conservation management.
Recognise how spatial and temporal scales impact efforts to conserve and manage biodiversity
Apply scientific principles and modern technologies to address current challenges faced by marine and terrestrial biodiversity.
Collaborate effectively within teams and engage professionally with stakeholders, including clients from the natural resource sector.
Communicate key concepts in conservation management effectively to industry standards.

courses.title: Advanced Concepts in Ecology 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL2051 Principles of Ecology 2
courses.aim: In this course students will understand and apply advanced ecological concepts, building on knowledge and concepts from Principles of Ecology 2. To do so, we explore conceptual and mechanistic models that aim to understand the dynamics of biological populations, communities and ecosystems. We then apply these models in a range of theoretical and applied scenarios in workshops. A mandatory field camp provides learners with hands-on experience and practical job-ready skills necessary for applying ecological principles in real-world environments. This course provides a crucial theoretical and applied understanding of ecological concepts for understanding the processes determining biodiversity in nature and its relevance for conservation and management. This course includes a compulsory field camp in the mid-semester break (see timetable). The field trips for Advanced Concepts in Ecology 3 and Freshwater Ecology 3 courses are scheduled back-to-back so that students can do both. Note that there is an additional cost associated with the camp, which varies year-to-year but is approximately 200-250 dollars.

clos.text: Explain and synthesise fundamental and advanced ecological concepts.
Analyse and evaluate complex ecological patterns and processes using contemporary conceptual and quantitative models.
Formulate specific research questions and design corresponding study designs to address existing knowledge gaps in ecology, both collaboratively and independently.
Collect high-quality ecological data in field settings and analyse using appropriate methods.
Communicate and justify ecological findings in relation to the broader scientific literature.

courses.title: Genetics 3B: Quantitative, Developmental and Medical Genetics
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of BIOL2005 Genetics 2A: Introduction to Genetic Analysis/BIOL2006 Genetics 2B: Applications of Genetic Analysis
courses.exclText: must not have completed BIOL3055 Gene Expression & Human & Developmental Genetics III
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to provide students with a comprehensive survey of concepts related to quantitative traits, the genetic determination of developmental pathways, the various types of human genetic mutation that lead to disease, the pathogenic pathways from genotype to phenotype and the legal regulatory framework for research in genetics.

clos.text: Explore the genetic basis of plant and invertebrate development and mammalian embryogenesis and analyse how evolution shapes developmental processes
Use genomic tools to perform genetic analysis for interpreting genetic basis and structure of quantitative trait variation in a population
Categorise different types of genetic disease based on their underlying causes and evaluate the genetic basis of cancer and its implications for diagnosis and treatment
Explain the basic principles of pharmacology and genomics as they pertain to pharmacogenetics and apply the available information resources for gene-drug interactions
Discuss legal and regulatory issues related to genetics research and address ethical dilemmas in genetic counselling and personalised medicine
Evaluate scientific research related to genetics as presented in peer-reviewed journal articles

courses.title: Marine and Wildlife Conservation
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL2051 Principles of Ecology 2
courses.exclText: must not have completed BIOL2009 Marine and Wildlife Conservation
courses.aim: The aim of the Marine and Wildlife Conservation course is to equip students with the investigative, analytical, and communication skills required for employment ready practice in conservation biology. Building on fieldwork and laboratory experiences in coastal and restoration environments, the curriculum challenges students to design and conduct independent and collaborative investigations, acquire and integrate ecological and social data, and communicate findings to diverse audiences. The course responds directly to employer feedback that South Australian graduates require greater capacity for independent organisation and critical thinking; accordingly, students are empowered to take ownership of their learning through self-directed inquiry, team-based research coordination, and the application of ecological principles to genuine conservation challenges facing marine and wildlife systems.

clos.text: Design, organise, and plan to conduct independent and collaborative investigations that evaluate conservation problems using ecological principles, including the assessment of coastal ecosystem dynamics and human impacts.

Acquire data from coastal habitats, laboratory methods and social interactions for the purposes of applying ecological concepts to evaluate biodiversity conservation challenges in marine and wildlife contexts.
Interpret and assess ecological data, social data, and their integration from coastal field studies or literature to judge the sustainable recovery of marine and wildlife systems.

Construct clear scientific outputs that communicate conservation findings to diverse audiences and collaborate in team‑based research by coordinating tasks, and where relevant integrate ecological and social evidence, and presenting insights from coastal ecosystems and restoration studies.

courses.title: Genetics Practical 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of BIOL2900 Molecular and Biomedical Science Practical 2/BIOL3006 Genetics 3A: Evolutionary Genetics and Epigenetics
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to provide students with a comprehensive survey of concepts related to quantitative traits, the genetic determination of developmental pathways, the various types of human genetic mutation that lead to disease, the pathogenic pathways from genotype to phenotype and the legal regulatory framework for research in genetics. This course expands from the foundation laid in Genetics IIA and IIB and presents cutting edge research topics in the field of developmental, quantitative, and human medical genetics.

clos.text: Demonstrate appropriate hands-on practical experimental skills for techniques frequently used in genetics research

Apply skills in experimental design to critically evaluation examples and/or design experiments to address complex genetic questions.
Work collaboratively in a team-based environment, demonstrating effective communication, project management, and problem-solving skills to achieve common goals
Perform laboratory techniques safely and according to legislative requirements

courses.title: Organic Chemistry 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed CHEM2001 Organic Chemistry 2
courses.aim: In this course, students will develop critical thinking, problem-solving and evaluative skills, in both theory-focussed workshops and practical based laboratory activities, in addition to technical laboratory skills, focussing on further developing an understanding of organic chemistry (determination of molecular structure from spectroscopic data, advanced organic reaction mechanisms, strategies and tactics in organic chemistry).

clos.text: Apply knowledge of interpretation of spectroscopic data, organic reaction mechanisms, and strategies and tactics in organic chemistry to conceptual problems, and to evaluate proposed solutions
Demonstrate proficiency in accurately representing chemical structures, formulae, equations and reaction mechanisms
Demonstrate proficiency in undertaking individual and/or team-based preparative laboratory investigations using appropriate apparatus, techniques and safe laboratory practices
Analyse, interpret and present the results of preparative laboratory experiments
Communicate results of laboratory experiment in written scientific reports and/or oral presentations
Design and plan an investigation by selecting and applying appropriate practical and/or theoretical techniques or tools

courses.title: Inorganic Chemistry 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed CHEM2002 Physical and Inorganic Chemistry 2
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to expand the learner’s knowledge of the distinct properties of metal-containing compounds from all areas of the periodic table, and to learn about the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of the reactions of metal complexes for the design of metal-containing drugs, imaging agents and catalysts. The course will also cover advanced magnetic and spectroscopic features of metal complexes and examine inorganic species with applications in facilitating our energy transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources. The laboratory course has been designed to provide learners with the practical skills necessary to carry out preparation, measurement and analysis of inorganic compounds, including the methods of modern instrumental analysis. Learners will develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills, together with evaluative skills, in both theory-focused workshops and practical-based laboratory sessions, in addition to technical laboratory skills. The course aims to develop in learners the ability to apply theoretical knowledge to practical problems and to handle complex data and equipment which aligns with key demands in scientific careers, equipping graduates to address real-world challenges effectively and to excel in various scientific sectors.

clos.text: Apply knowledge of inorganic and organometallic reaction mechanisms, solid-state chemistry, and advanced spectroscopy and magnetism to analyse and solve conceptual and quantitative problems, and to evaluate proposed solutions
Accurately represent chemical structures, formulae, equations and reaction mechanisms
Prepare for undertaking individual and/or team-based preparative and measurement-based laboratory investigations using safe laboratory practices
Demonstrate proficiency in conducting individual and/or team-based preparative and measurement-based laboratory investigations using appropriate apparatus and techniques
Analyse, interpret and present the results of measurement-based laboratory experiments
Communicate ideas that relate to inorganic and organometallic reaction mechanisms, solid-state chemistry, and advanced spectroscopy and magnetism in written and/or oral form to specialist audiences

courses.title: Physical Chemistry 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of CHEM2002 Physical and Inorganic Chemistry 2/MATH1004 Calculus 1 OR must have completed equivalent courses
prereqNotes: equivalent courses
courses.aim: In this course, students will develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills in both theory-focussed workshops and practical based laboratory activities, in addition to technical laboratory and computational skills, focussing on developing a deep understanding of core aspects of physical chemistry.

clos.text: Apply knowledge of advanced quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics and kinetics, and electronic and nuclear spectroscopy to conceptual and quantitative problems
Evaluate the appropriateness of different computational techniques and numerical approximations for solving physical chemistry problems
Demonstrate proficiency in accurately representing chemical structures, formulae and equations
Demonstrate proficiency in undertaking individual and/or team-based measurement-based laboratory investigations using appropriate apparatus, techniques and safe laboratory practices
