Interrogate how airborne and spaceborne imaging sensors can provide spatial information for environmental management
Describe the spatial variability of the biophysical environment and analyse how it affects the sustainable use of natural resources
Demonstrate the use of GIS for independent, critical, and creative agricultural or NRM research

courses.title: Environmental Pollution and Monitoring
excl: ENVT4031 at the University of South Australia
courses.exclText: must not have completed ENVT4031 at the University of South Australia
courses.aim: The broad aim is to equip students with the practical skills and knowledge to plan and undertake environmental monitoring programs. This includes coverage of key pollution concepts, toxicology and ecotoxicology principles, major classes of pollutants, the science of monitoring for environmental quality assessment, environmental legislation and risk assessment perspectives. The course is “hands on”, where students learn by undertaking activities on environmental sampling, processing and instrumental analysis methods, which mimic the real world, thus delivering an authentic learning experience, aligning with the program’s intent to prepare students for professional practice.

clos.text: Explain key concepts relating to pollution and apply these to specific contaminants
Explain the chemistry (i.e. reactions, structures or associations) of major types of contaminants, including their sources and adverse effects on organisms, structures or environmental services
Design and present a monitoring and reporting program to investigate specific pollution of an environmental system.
Accurately collect, process, and analyse environmental samples, then summarise and interpret the results in a written report and an oral presentation.

courses.title: GIS for Environmental Management
courses.exclText: must not have completed ENVI3008
courses.aim: In this course, students will learn the background science and application skills in geographic information systems with a special emphasis on environmental management.

clos.text: Demonstrate proficiency in using ArcGIS for spatial data preparation, analysis and visualisation
Demonstrate proficiency in vector and raster processing
Interrogate how airborne and spaceborne imaging sensors can provide spatial information for environmental management
Quantitatively describe the spatial variability of the biophysical environment
Demonstrate the use of GIS for independent, critical, and creative environmental research

courses.title: Environmental Technologies 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed CHEM1004 Introduction to Environmental Chemistry OR must have completed AGRI2004 Soil and Water Resources 2 OR must have completed EART2011 Geochemistry 2
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to provide students with an in-depth understanding of the various technologies available for the prevention, treatment and remediation of environmental issues in air, soil and water systems. The course will cover technologies and approaches related to carbon capture, storage and sequestration, contaminated land remediation, mine site rehabilitation, treatment and recycling of nutrient from waste streams. Students will learn about existing and emerging technologies and assess whether they provide solutions with meaningful results for the environment.

clos.text: Outline and discuss the theoretical basis for a range of technological solutions aimed at mitigating and repairing societal influences on the carbon cycle
Undertake basic calculations to assess the impact, practical applicability and/or validity of various environmental technologies
Integrate existing scientific knowledge, information and datasets to outline solutions to environmental quality problems at a given site/locality
Work as part of a team to research and assess technology solutions
Provide recommendations for the implementation of technology solutions and/or outline considerations for government policy development
Communicate scientific findings in a professional manner

courses.title: Environmental and Geospatial Field Project
excl: ENVT3030 at the University of South Australia
courses.exclText: must not have completed ENVT3030 at the University of South Australia
courses.aim: This course will provide students with the skills and confidence necessary to create and implement a project for the solution of a natural resource management problem and to act as a consultant in presenting the project to the management agency. Students work cooperatively with management agencies and staff supervisors to apply what they have learned throughout the program to address specific resource management issues using a multidisciplinary approach. Within the framework of a project brief, students work to: define values and issues, collect and analyse data, investigate and plan problem solving strategies, prepare comprehensive guidelines including financing strategies, and present a proposal pitch. This course will typically include a 75-hour field experience or industry placement.

clos.text: Design a project proposal that addresses a specific problem within a set of economic and resource constraints.
Manage a project efficiently and effectively from problem identification through to the development and communication of recommendations.
Create a feasible and sustainable solution to a given problem that takes account of international trends in environmental management.
Present a professional written and oral report to a specific stakeholder group.
Reflect on ways to improve project management and project outcomes.

courses.title: Environmental and Social Impact Assessment
excl: ENVT2014 Environmental and Social Impact Assessment at the University of South Australia
courses.exclText: must not have completed ENVT2014 Environmental and Social Impact Assessment at the University of South Australia
courses.aim: Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) is widely applied throughout the world to assess and predict potential adverse social and environmental impacts and to develop suitable mitigation measures for major development projects. At a broader level, strategic EISA can be used by governments to plan where and what sort of developments might be best located in different places. The course aims to provide an overview of these and a detailed examination of the processes involved in ESIA and how these can be used effectively in environmental management. The course will also examine key environmental management legislation in South Australia and at the Commonwealth level, with an overall aim of producing critically aware practitioners who are able to manage ESIA at a strategic or project level.

courses.title: Food Processing and Manufacturing
courses.prereqText: must have completed FOODX500 Food Microbiology
excl: FOSC3002 at University of South Australia
FOOD SC3580WT at University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed FOSC3002 at University of South Australia OR must not have completed FOOD SC3580WT at University of Adelaide
courses.assumed: Students are expected to have foundational knowledge and skills typically developed in food science or related science courses. This includes a basic understanding of food composition, simple chemical and biological principles relevant to food systems, and introductory concepts in food processing and food safety. Students should be able to perform basic laboratory measurements, record and interpret simple experimental data, apply elementary mathematical calculations, and engage with scientific literature at an introductory level. No advanced technical or engineering knowledge is assumed. Core processing concepts and calculations required for the course are introduced and developed within the course.
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to provide students with an understanding of the principles and applications of food processing and manufacturing operations used in modern food production systems. The course examines the scientific, engineering, quality, safety, sustainability, and regulatory aspects of food processing, packaging, and preservation technologies. Students develop the knowledge and skills required to evaluate food manufacturing processes, assess the impact of processing on food quality and safety, and critically examine emerging technologies used within the food industry.

clos.text: Explain the principles underlying various food unit operations used in food processing and manufacturing
Interpret and calculate thermal and related food processing data relevant to food industry
Analyse and evaluate specific aspects of food processing, and manufacturing operations for selected food products using critical thinking to optimise processing conditions and mitigate risks
Explain the principles and applications of food packaging systems and packaging material selection in relation to food safety, shelf life, sustainability, and global food supply chains.
Evaluate the impacts of conventional and emerging food processing, manufacturing, and packaging techniques on the physical, chemical, microbiological, sensory, and nutritional quality of foods
Explain the principles of Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), wastewater management, and relevant food industry regulations in the context of food manufacturing operations.

courses.title: Food Product Development 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of FOOD3015 Advanced Food Microbiology/FOODX200 Sensory Evaluations of Food
courses.aim: Students will learn how to design, formulate, produce and package market foods under industry conditions which are relevant to the Australian marketplace.

clos.text: Demonstrate technical understanding and practical skillset across all stages of food product development, from ideation to launch.
Apply regulatory frameworks for quality assurance, including good manufacturing practice (GMP), hazard assessment, and critical control point (HACCP).

Describe the functionality of suitable packaging materials, and apply food label standards, including regulations for Nutrition- and Health-related claims, in compliance with the Food Standards Code (FSANZ).

Investigate and critically evaluate new food trends, including novel processing technologies, First Nations’ foods, sustainability, value-adding, food reformulation and marketing concepts, and explore areas for innovation.
Work collaboratively with others to develop an innovative food product from concept to prototype, and effectively analyse, evaluate and scientifically communicate findings.

courses.title: Future Foods
courses.aim: This course aims to provide an overview of contemporary transformations and innovations in nutrition and food production for creating global sustainable future food systems. The purpose of the course is to provide up to date information on new, upcoming, and innovative foods, alternative protein sources, and food production technologies and to better understand the factors which contribute to a sustainable food system from a food science, nutrition, environmental, and economic perspective.

clos.text: Describe technological innovations in future food production and the impact of food sources on the global sustainability of food systems
Characterise and describe Australian native Indigenous food systems, including food sources and their bioactive components
Critically evaluate the environmental, social, and economic impacts of different food production methods
Develop creative solutions to address the environmental, economic, and ethical dimensions of contemporary food issues
Demonstrate high level communication skills in translating evidence on modern food production and sustainability

courses.title: Brewing Technology and Beer Production 3
excl: FOODSC3550WT Brewing Technology & Beer Production III at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed CHEM4007 Brewery Engineering (UoA) OR must not have completed FOODSC3550WT Brewing Technology & Beer Production III at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: Brewing Technology and Beer Production III will offer students a comprehensive introduction to the science and technology underpinning the composition and manufacture of beer. Students will gain a detailed theoretical understanding of the role of the raw ingredients of beer production (water, fermentable materials, flavouring materials, yeasts and bacteria) and the processes by which these are used in beer formulation and creation. Through participation in sensory classes, compulsory visits to industrial sites including maltings and large and small-scale breweries, and practical exercises in brewing at small and intermediate scales, students will become familiar with all aspects of beer production, and be able to design, brew and evaluate beers.

clos.text: Discuss the role of the major raw ingredients in beer composition and its sensory properties.
Explain the processes by which the raw ingredients are transformed during the brewing process.
Identify the tastes, flavours and aromas associated with the key international beer styles in modern production.
Identify the major faults in beers, and describe the practices for minimisation of microbial and oxidative spoilage.
Plan and implement the production of beer according to a selected style.
Work in a group to prepare and critique written and oral presentations

courses.title: Advanced Food Microbiology
courses.prereqText: must have completed FOODX500 Food Microbiology
courses.aim: This course provides advanced knowledge of the ecology, physiology, and functionality of microorganisms in food systems, with emphasis on food quality, food safety, and public health. Students investigate microbial adaptation, food spoilage, fermentation, emerging microbiological hazards, and food-associated microbiomes using contemporary microbiological and molecular approaches, including whole genome sequencing. The course develops the knowledge and practical skills required to apply predictive microbiology and risk-based food safety management, including quantitative microbial risk assessment, and to interpret and communicate evidence-based solutions to complex food microbiology challenges within scientific, regulatory, ethical, and sustainability contexts.

clos.text: Critically evaluate the ecology, physiology, and adaptive stress responses of microorganisms within food, food processing, and gastrointestinal ecosystems.
Analyse the mechanisms by which microorganisms contribute to food spoilage, fermentation, food safety, and human health outcomes.
Apply contemporary microbiological and molecular approaches, including sequencing-based technologies, to investigate, detect, and characterise microorganisms relevant to food quality and safety.
Evaluate emerging microbiological hazards, including foodborne pathogens, viruses, antimicrobial-resistant microorganisms, and microbiota-associated risks within food systems.

Apply risk-based approaches, including microbiological sampling plans, Food Safety Objectives (FSOs), predictive microbiology, and quantitative microbial risk assessment (QMRA), to assess and manage food safety risks.
Design, interpret and communicate evidence-based solutions to complex food microbiology challenges, integrating scientific, regulatory, public health, ethical, and sustainability considerations.

courses.title: Food Science Placement
courses.prereqText: must have completed Students must have completed 96 units of study in the Bachelor of Science Food Science and Technology major (FOODBSCIE)
prereqNotes: Students must have completed 96 units of study in the Bachelor of Science Food Science and Technology major (FOODBSCIE)
courses.exclText: must not have completed all of SCIE3014 STEM Internship (140 hours)/SCIE3900 Science Professional Placement
courses.aim: To provide Bachelor of Science (Food Science and Technology) students with the opportunity to undertake a structured, industry-aligned placement that develops their professional skills within the food sector aligned to the course learning outcomes. Through the completion of 120 hours of placement in an approved setting and the maintenance of an industry project report, students will consolidate their learnings and practical experience and enhance their professional readiness.

clos.text: Apply disciplinary and professional knowledge in a real-world food industry workplace to contribute effectively to routine tasks, projects, or operations under supervision.

Demonstrate appropriate workplace behaviours, including communication, teamwork, time management, and adherence to industry safety, ethical, and professional standards as appropriate to the specific sector of the food industry.

Collect, document, analyse [BW1.1]and critically reflect on workplace experiences, learning and projects in a structured report and/or presentation, identifying links between theory and practice in the food sector.
Evaluate personal strengths, skill development, and career aspirations in relation to the food industry, identifying areas for further professional growth and employability development.

courses.title: Food Production in a Future Climate
excl: PLANT SC3530WT at The University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed PLANT SC3530WT at The University of Adelaide
courses.aim: Students will develop an appreciation for the complexity of natural resource management issues and their impact on agricultural production and societal change. This will be achieved by providing an in-depth understanding of the impacts of global climate change on plant growth with specific focus on how climate change is likely to affect food production. Crops and agricultural systems of particular importance to Australian agricultural and horticultural production will be closely examined. The course will highlight the importance of understanding the mechanisms by which a changing climate will affect plant performance and food production. Changing phenology, plant species range shifts, changing pest pressure and variation in yield will be explored in the context of climate change. This course integrates concepts of physiology, biochemistry, genetics, agronomy, and pest management gained by students in previous courses thus developing an in-depth understanding of the drivers of climate change and how future prediction models are generated. Students will develop skills in critical analysis of data and literature to enable them to make informed decisions relating to future food production.

clos.text: Describe the natural and anthropogenic causes for climate variation and the impacts on key plant processes such as phenology, photosynthesis, respiration and growth
Understand the concepts and limitations in the global climate models that are used to predict future climate scenarios
Understand the implications of changing climate on plant production in a range of cropping systems

Apply knowledge about the response of plants to climate change to specific agricultural and horticultural species and predict the production outcomes or the locations best suited for production systems in future climate scenarios
Source and critically analyse relevant peer reviewed literature
Communicate aspects of climate change science to their peers in accessible language

courses.title: Environmental Law
courses.aim: This elective course equips students to address the local, national and global environmental challenges that are critical to a sustainable future. Students will be introduced to the concepts and principles that underpin environmental law at the international and federal levels, and state and local levels in South Australia. As graduate lawyers, they will be able to provide leadership on the legal dimensions to environmental problems and the social, economic and cultural effects of environmental damage. Students will study and reflect on current and emerging environmental issues and the response of the law, and learn about the constraints of federalism in the legal responses that impact matters such as environmental planning, development control and protection of biological diversity. They will gain knowledge, skills, and attributes to develop innovative legal solutions informed by cross-disciplinary perspectives.

clos.text: Identify relevant principles of international, federal and state environmental protection laws in legislation, regulations and case law; and apply these principles to provide advice in relation to an environmental problem
Demonstrate knowledge of the state and federal powers, functions, responsibilities and institutions relating to Australian Environmental Law
Research, explain, critically analyse and reflect on the role of law in promoting environmental sustainability and addressing environmental issues

courses.title: Public Health and Community Nutrition
courses.prereqText: must have completed NUTR2001 Lifespan Nutrition Physiology
courses.aim: This course develops students' understanding of public health nutrition with a focus placed on the importance of building a sustainable, nutritious, and healthy food supply for all. Consideration is given to factors and health inequities which influence consumer food choices, including social, cultural, and environmental factors. An overview of the different types of food systems as well as historical events which influence the Australian diet over time, are used to illustrate how people's day-to-day living circumstances can impact on their dietary patterns. Major nutrition and health policies which underpin intervention programs and initiatives aiming to promote healthy eating behaviours will be explored. The course aligns with the program intent to promote innovation and evidence-based nutrition practices with consideration of social realties to improve the health of Australians.

clos.text: Demonstrate how food choices and eating patterns impact the nutritional health of individuals and populations
Critically examine food systems and the development of sustainable and healthy food supplies
Translate and apply current food and nutrition policies and initiatives to real-world contexts
Appraise information from a wide variety of sources, emphasising core concepts around impediments and enablers to the nutritional health of populations
Formulate and design an innovative community nutrition intervention

courses.title: Drug Development 2
courses.prereqText: must have completed PHAR2007 Drug Development 1
excl: PHAR3013 Drug Development 2 at the University of South Australia
courses.exclText: must not have completed PHAR3013 Drug Development 2 at the University of South Australia
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to further extend prior knowledge of drug discovery in the critical evaluation of the major phases of the drug development process and apply this knowledge to the commercialisation aspects of a new drug program. Intellectual property and patenting in the pharmaceutical industry; ownership of knowledge, ownership of information, IP protection. Clinical trials insight into industry. Diagnostics and Personalised medicine. Regulatory affairs; filing a New Drug Application (NDA); the evaluation of an NDA by the Food and Drug Administration and the Therapeutics Goods Administration. The use of data in drug development. Pharmaceutical commercialisation: how companies are funded; private and public funding of the pharmaceutical industry; spin-off and start-up companies; Ethical behaviour in pharmaceutical commercialisation; Role of pharmacoeconomics in strategic drug development.

clos.text: Apply knowledge of drug discovery and development to evaluate the key data and contributors towards the successful commercialisation of a pharmaceutical product.
Demonstrate an awareness of the different types of funding available to commercialise pharmaceutical products and the costs and timelines of the process.
Describe the relationship between regulatory requirements, industry needs, and drug efficacy and safety.
Understand the importance of patents for the protection of intellectual property, be able to run a patent search, and subsequently interpret the major sections and their significance.
Demonstrate the ethical and cultural issues surrounding bio-prospecting and the rights of Indigenous peoples.
Apply the methods used to assign a commercial value to a pharmaceutical project and to a pharmaceutical company.

courses.title: Electromagnetism, Quantum and Statistical Mechanics
courses.prereq: (MATHX202 AND MATHX203 AND PHYS2001 AND PHYS2002)
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of MATHX202 Differential Equations/MATHX203 Multivariable Calculus/PHYS2001 Quantum Mechanics and Experimental Physics 2/PHYS2002 Electromagnetism 2
excl: PHYSICS3542 at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed PHYSICS3542 at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: This course enables students to develop concepts in quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics and electromagnetism with mathematical rigour such that the behaviour of the physical universe can be understood from a fundamental perspective.

clos.text: Define the concepts introduced in quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics and electromagnetism and explain how they are related
Use the knowledge in each of these areas of study to explain relevant aspects of the physical world
Use the mathematical techniques relevant to each area of study to solve straightforward and complex problems
Use computational methods to solve relevant problems that do not have an analytical solution
Work cooperatively in a team to develop an understanding of concepts and solve problems
Use the tools, methodologies, language and conventions of physics to communicate ideas and explanations

courses.title: Optics and Photonics 3
courses.prereq: (MATHX202 AND MATHX203 AND PHYS2002 AND PHYS2003)
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of MATHX202 Differential Equations/MATHX203 Multivariable Calculus/PHYS2002 Electromagnetism 2/PHYS2003 Solid State Physics and Photonics 2
excl: PHYSICS 3540 at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed PHYSICS 3540 at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: This course provides students with a knowledge of optics and photonics.

clos.text: Describe and explain the paraxial scalar wave equation, and the integral, Gaussian and guided mode solutions;
Apply wave optics to a range of problems;
Describe, explain and apply the Fresnel equation for the reflection and transmission of light for isotropic and anisotropic non-conducting media;
Describe and explain the operation of common optical components;
Describe and explain the structure and operation of simple lasers;
Use the tools, methodologies, language and conventions of physics to test and communicate ideas and explanations

courses.title: Advanced Dynamics and Relativity
courses.prereq: (MATHX202 AND MATHX203 AND PHYS2002 AND PHYS2004)
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of MATHX202 Differential Equations/MATHX203 Multivariable Calculus/PHYS2002 Electromagnetism 2/PHYS2004 Classical Physics 2
excl: PHYSICS 3006 at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed PHYSICS 3006 at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: This course enables students to develop a working knowledge of analytical mechanics and relativity to the standard required for further study in physics.

clos.text: Apply variational methods, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics, and conservation laws to formulate and solve problems in classical mechanics.
Analyse dynamical systems using Noether's theorem, normal modes, Hamiltonian mechanics, and Poisson brackets.
Apply the mathematical framework of special relativity, including space-time, four-vectors, and tensors, to solve relativistic mechanics problems.
Apply covariant formulations of electromagnetism to analyse relativistic electrodynamics using Maxwell's equations and the electromagnetic field tensor.
Communicate mathematical reasoning and physical interpretations clearly and accurately through analytical problem solving and scientific writing.

courses.title: Solid State Physics 3
courses.prereq: (MATHX202 AND MATHX203 AND PHYS2001 AND PHYS2002)
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of MATHX202 Differential Equations/MATHX203 Multivariable Calculus/PHYS2001 Quantum Mechanics and Experimental Physics 2/PHYS2002 Electromagnetism 2
courses.aim: Our understanding of the physical properties of solids provides the foundation for future fundamental research and the development of new technology. Much of technology in our world is founded in the use and understanding of materials, particularly solids. The systematic study of the physics of solids is known as solid state physics. This course introduces students to this large and broad field of physics. This includes the electrical, thermal, magnetic and optical properties of solids, their crystal and electronic structure, and their application in science, engineering, and medicine.

clos.text: Explain at a high level the major concepts in solid-state physics;
Describe the important concepts of crystal structure, reciprocal space, single-particle band-structure, and the difference between semiconductors and metals;
Describe examples of solid-state physics applications in modern technology;
Tangible problem solving: write the operational equations of solid-state problems to be solved;
Demonstrate effective oral and written communication skills

courses.title: Advanced Quantum Mechanics
courses.prereqText: must have completed PHYS3002 Electromagnetism, Quantum and Statistical Mechanics
courses.aim: This course develops a deeper understanding of quantum mechanics through its formal structure, key approximation methods, and applications to physical systems. It builds on prior study of quantum mechanics by establishing a more complete operator-based framework, exploring symmetries and conservation laws, and developing tools for analysing realistic systems. Emphasis is placed on connecting mathematical structure to physical interpretation and on solving problems relevant to atomic, nuclear, and particle physics. The course prepares students for advanced study by strengthening analytical reasoning and theoretical problem-solving skills.

clos.text: Apply the formal principles of quantum mechanics to analyse and model physical systems.
Solve quantum mechanical problems using appropriate analytical techniques and approximation methods.
Analyse quantum systems using operator methods, symmetry principles and mathematical representations of quantum states.
Communicate quantum mechanical reasoning and calculations using appropriate mathematical notation and physical interpretation.

courses.title: Atmospheric and Astrophysics 3
courses.prereq: (MATHX202 AND MATHX203 AND PHYS2001 AND PHYS2002)
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of MATHX202 Differential Equations/MATHX203 Multivariable Calculus/PHYS2001 Quantum Mechanics and Experimental Physics 2/PHYS2002 Electromagnetism 2
excl: PHYSICS3532 at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed PHYSICS3532 at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: This course allows students to develop their knowledge of modern techniques, theory and observational results relating to energetic processes in astrophysics and cosmology and introduces the physics of planetary atmospheres with special emphasis on the atmosphere of the Earth.

clos.text: Analyse and apply core physical principles to account for key phenomena in astrophysics.
Apply physical principles to analyse atmospheric structure, motion, and climate processes.
Select, apply, and evaluate appropriate analytical, numerical, or computational methods to solve physics problems.
Communicate physics reasoning using appropriate tools, conventions, and representations.

courses.title: Computational Physics
courses.prereq: (MATHX202 AND MATHX203 AND PHYS2001 AND PHYS2002)
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of MATHX202 Differential Equations/MATHX203 Multivariable Calculus/PHYS2001 Quantum Mechanics and Experimental Physics 2/PHYS2002 Electromagnetism 2
excl: PHYSICS 3534 Computational Physics III at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed PHYSICS 3534 Computational Physics III at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: This hands-on course introduces computational methods in solving problems in physics. It teaches programming tactics, numerical methods and their implementation, together with methods of linear algebra.

clos.text: Describe modern programming methods and their capabilities and limitations in physics applications.
Identify and describe the characteristics of various numerical methods.
Establish tactics for encapsulating and hiding complexity.
Independently program computers using leading-edge tools.
Formulate and solve computationally a selection of problems in physics.
Use the tools, methodologies, language and conventions of physics to test and communicate ideas and explanations.
Decide the appropriate paradigm for addressing current computational physics challenges.

courses.title: Experimental Physics
courses.prereq: (MATHX202 AND MATHX203 AND PHYS2001 AND PHYS2002)
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of MATHX202 Differential Equations/MATHX203 Multivariable Calculus/PHYS2001 Quantum Mechanics and Experimental Physics 2/PHYS2002 Electromagnetism 2
excl: PHYSICS 3002 at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed PHYSICS 3002 at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: In this advanced experimental course, students engage in experiments in selected areas including atomic and nuclear physics, optics and electromagnetism. They also complete a practical analogue electronics component.

clos.text: Describe key components of analogue electronics including transistors and operational amplifiers and their use in electronic filtering and waveform generation.
Conduct experiments to investigate important physics phenomena.
Use a digital oscilloscope that is interfaced to a computer to optimally sample a waveform and utilise fast Fourier techniques to understand the signal.

Keep a scientific record of experimental work, analyse the results of experiments, and use appropriate techniques to estimate the experimental uncertainty associated with measurements, to reach non-trivial conclusions about the experiment.
Work cooperatively in a team to solve practical problems.
Use the tools, methodologies, language and conventions of physics to test and communicate ideas and explanations.

courses.title: Nuclear and Radiation Physics 3
courses.prereq: (MATHX202 AND MATHX203 AND PHYS2001 AND PHYS2002)
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of MATHX202 Differential Equations/MATHX203 Multivariable Calculus/PHYS2001 Quantum Mechanics and Experimental Physics 2/PHYS2002 Electromagnetism 2
courses.exclText: must not have completed PHYSICS7011 (UoA)
courses.aim: This course extends the concepts of nuclear physics and theoretical and applied radiation physics.

clos.text: Describe fundamental aspects of the structure of the nucleus, radioactive decay, nuclear reactions and the interaction of radiation and matter and explain them in terms of applicable principles of physics.
Apply knowledge of nuclear and radiation physics and appropriate mathematics to formulate solutions to problems.
Discuss the connection of nuclear and radiation physics with other physics disciplines - solid state, elementary particle physics, radiochemistry, astronomy.
Describe applications of nuclear and radiation physics in medical diagnostics and therapy, astrophysics, geology, archaeology and other fields.

Describe experimental techniques used (or developed) for nuclear physics purposes (logic circuits, gamma cameras, semiconductor detectors) and discuss their influence on the development of new technologies.
Explore an application of nuclear and/or radiation physics and communicate their understanding to a group of their peers in a short presentation.

courses.title: Environment and Citizenship
courses.aim: This course explores the ways in which environmental concerns are reshaping our understanding of citizenship as well as how the language of citizenship (e.g. rights and duties) is shaping environmental politics and policies around the world, including Australia. The first part introduces students to concepts and theories of citizenship. The second part explores the practical manifestations of environmental citizenship, with specific attention to three major political actors: citizens, governments, and corporations. The course provides students with a variety of analytical tools to interpret and assess environmental issues and develop skills to engage in political discourse and policymaking regarding environmental sustainability.

clos.text: Understand the different conceptions of environmental citizenship
Identify and discuss the challenges faced by environmental citizenship
Think critically about the many manifestations of environmental citizenship
Conduct independent research utilising a variety of sources
Produce coherent and well substantiated arguments
Express ideas confidently, thoughtfully and respectfully

courses.title: Infrastructure and Sustainability
courses.aim: The objective of the course is to develop an understanding of tangible ways to improve the economic, social, and environmental performance of urban infrastructure across the design, construction and operation phases. The course will cover a range of topics relevant to current sustainable infrastructure challenges with a focus on the integration of the development, transport and energy sectors. The course is delivered in an interactive industry style small group discovery model and provides students with valuable industry ready knowledge and skills.

clos.text: Discuss how sustainability outcomes can be improved in particular forms of infrastructure that align to specific global and national best practice principles
Understand a range of factors that drive good outcomes in infrastructure sustainability with a focus on responding to climate change
Compare and contrast national government approaches to sustainable infrastructure planning
Discuss key sustainable infrastructure messages from the Australian Infrastructure Audit and Australian Infrastructure Plan and identify examples of best practice
Discuss the sustainability implications of electro-mobility and the integration of transport and land use planning
Identify specific implications for sustainable infrastructure from the transition from centralised to distributed energy networks

courses.title: Project Logistics and Supply Chains
courses.prereqText: must have completed all of PROJ1000 Foundations of Project Management/PROJ1001 Scheduling and Cost Management
courses.aim: This course aims to build an understanding of system support planning and logistics support over a project life-cycle. Furthermore, the implications of an extended supply chain are to be considered. The course will teach topics in respect to the components of logistics, logistics engineering and management, system design for supportability and continued assessment. Other areas that are covered include supply chain integration, information flows, materials, services, human resources and supply chain monetary aspects, tiered suppliers and technology coordination, supply chain enterprise architecture and waste minimisation.

clos.text: Describe the concept of “systems” across the logistics and supply chain project life-cycle
Plan supportability requirements for the development of logistics and supply chains systems
Identify design techniques and technologies that support logistics and extended supply chains
Work effectively in teams on logistical systems and supply chain development
Recognise ethical, social and cultural issues within logistics and supply chains

courses.title: Human Behaviour and Conservation 3
courses.prereqText: must have completed 1 of BIOL1032 Ecological Issues 1/ENVI2007 Environmental Interpretation and Community Engagement
courses.aim: This course aims to enable students to critically explore human behaviour as it relates to conservation and barriers to environmentally responsibly behaviours.Using a psychological perspective, students will evaluate strategies to facilitate behaviour change in support of conservation of the natural environment.

clos.text: Explain key psychological principles of advertising and persuasion, core principles of behaviour change, and ethical considerations relevant to their application in conservation and marketing contexts
Analyse contemporary marketing materials and conservation initiatives to determine how psychological principles are applied to influence human behaviours.
Interpret and evaluate behaviour data using appropriate measurement approaches and analytical concepts relevant to conservation behaviour change.

Critically evaluates current conservation research to identify a threat or problem relevant to the conservation of a species or environment that may be addressed through ethical human behaviour change.
Design a conservation strategy centred on a specific human behaviour that demonstrates understanding in persuasive communication, psychological principles, and community based social marketing

courses.title: Web Cartography
courses.prereqText: must have completed ENGI2004 Spatial Data Acquisition and Analysis
excl: GEOE3019 at the University of South Australia
courses.exclText: must not have completed GEOE3019 at the University of South Australia
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to further develop theoretical and practical skills in Geospatial Science while focusing on designing, creating, publishing and evaluation of user-centric or purpose-oriented interactive web mapping applications. This course is designed for students to enhance their acquired knowledge to analyse and communicate geospatial information effectively and efficiently through a web browser. Students will gain skills in internet map creation, cartographic web map design, and communication with online maps. Ultimately, this course aims to develop the ability to apply theoretical knowledge to practical problems and to create and communicate insight into complex spatial data which aligns with key demands in scientific careers, equipping graduates to address real-world challenges effectively and to excel in various scientific sectors.

clos.text: Apply knowledge of cartographic design principles for interactive web maps and mapping applications
Prepare and pre-process geographic data for web-based rendering
Apply web-based spatial analysis for real-time geographic information gathering
Design and create effective and readable interactive web maps and mapping applications to communicate insight into discipline specific data and topics
Conceptualise and conduct user, usage and usability test to evaluate web mapping products
Communicate the process of Web mapping in oral, written and digital format and then critically reflect upon the process to further professional development

courses.title: Topics in Forensic Science
courses.aim: The aim of this course is to give students an overview of the area of forensic sciences including pathology, toxicology, anthropology and odontology, and provide an insight into how they may be used to investigate crime. The topics that will be covered include the changes in the body with death and decomposition; the pathology of wounds; burns; disaster victim identification; sudden death in children and adults; medical misadventure and drug-related deaths. As well as introducing students to content, emphasis is placed on applying critical thinking to analyse hypothetical cases and scenarios.

clos.text: Describe the basis of forensic science and pathology and how these areas interact with the law, using specific forensic terminology
Describe how crime scene investigations, together with forensic toxicology, forensic anthropology, forensic odontology, drug and DNA analysis, can support the investigation of serious crime
Analyse the features of injuries and injury patterns associated with burns, drowning, electrocution, asphyxia and firearms
Explain the types and features of natural and unnatural deaths, including those due to medical conditions, homicides, suicides, accidental deaths and sudden infant death syndrome
Recognise the relevant issues in a hypothetical forensic scenario to determine how investigators would proceed with an investigation
Critically analyse and interpret published scientific literature

courses.title: Communicating Science 3
courses.aim: Communicating Science equips students with the essential skills and knowledge to effectively communicate scientific concepts to diverse audiences. This course is designed for students who are passionate about bridging the gap between science and society through effective communication and welcomes students from various disciplines, including sciences, humanities, and social sciences. Upon successfully completing Communicating Science, students will be equipped with the skills, knowledge, and attitudes necessary to excel in science communication roles and contribute to fostering public understanding of science. Students will be prepared for diverse career opportunities in science journalism, public relations, science advocacy, science policy, museum curation, and other related fields. Students will hone their written communication abilities by producing compelling content suitable for diverse publications, including blogs, press releases, and feature articles. They will also refine their oral communication skills, through delivering captivating speeches and learning how to distill complex ideas into concise soundbites. Off-campus excursions to science exhibitions will provide students with firsthand experiences in science communication outside written and oral forms. Students will observe and analyse different communication strategies employed in these settings, enhancing their understanding of engaging diverse audiences and making complex scientific concepts accessible and relevant. By successfully completing these assessments, students will demonstrate their ability to communicate science effectively, responsibly, and ethically.

clos.text: Show awareness and understanding of the background, fundamentals and theory of traditional and emerging media and how these relate to the communication of science.
Produce written communication suitable for a variety of media and publications.
Demonstrate oral communication skills from speeches to soundbites.
Demonstrate online communication skills from blog posts to videos.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the scope and diversity of science communication.
Demonstrate responsible, ethical and respectful attitudes as the field undergoes disruptive change fuelled by rapid technology advancement.

courses.title: Science International Study Tour
excl: SCIENCE3500 Science International Study Tour at the University of Adelaide
courses.exclText: must not have completed SCIENCE3500 Science International Study Tour at the University of Adelaide
courses.aim: This course consists of an intensive overseas study tour introducing science students to international culture and society and providing an opportunity to visit an overseas partner institution, participate in academic seminars and/or cultural activities. The course is designed to develop students' skills in observation, reflection, induction, and deduction on discipline-specific issues in an international context, develop graduates' knowledge of international affairs, and gain confidence to work in one of a range of international environments. The focus of the student's intellectual attention will be her/his participation in a group activity influencing a scientific-related system and conducted outside of Australia. courses.title: Communicating Science
courses.prereqText: must have completed 96 units of undergraduate study or equivalent
prereqNotes: 96 units of undergraduate study or equivalent
courses.exclText: must not have completed EART4004 Communicating Science/SCIE3008 Communicating Science 3/SCIE5001 Communicating Science (PG)/SCIENCE3200, SCIENCE4020 or SCIENCE7020 at University of Adelaide
courses.aim: Communicating Science equips students with the essential skills and knowledge to effectively communicate scientific concepts to diverse audiences. This course is designed for students who are passionate about bridging the gap between science and society through effective communication and welcomes students from various disciplines, including sciences, humanities, and social sciences. Upon successfully completing Communicating Science, students will be equipped with the skills, knowledge, and attitudes necessary to excel in science communication roles and contribute to fostering public understanding of science. Students will be prepared for diverse career opportunities in science journalism, public relations, science advocacy, science policy, museum curation, and other related fields. Students will hone their written communication abilities by producing compelling content suitable for diverse publications, including blogs, press releases, and feature articles. They will also refine their oral communication skills through delivering captivating speeches and learning how to distil complex ideas into concise soundbites. Off-campus excursions to science exhibitions will provide students with firsthand experiences in science communication outside written and oral forms. Students will observe and analyse different communication strategies employed in these settings, enhancing their understanding of engaging diverse audiences and making complex scientific concepts accessible and relevant. By successfully completing these assessments, students will demonstrate their ability to communicate science effectively, responsibly, and ethically.

clos.text: Show awareness and understanding of the background, fundamentals and theory of traditional and emerging media and how these relate to the communication of science.
Produce written communication suitable for a variety of media and publications.
Demonstrate oral communication skills from speeches to soundbites.
Demonstrate online communication skills from blog posts to videos.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the scope and diversity of science communication.
Demonstrate responsible, ethical and respectful attitudes as the field undergoes disruptive change fuelled by rapid technology advancement.

courses.title: Protein Purification: Principles and Practice
courses.prereqText: must have completed BIOL2017 Biochemistry 2: Molecular and Cellular Biology
courses.exclText: must not have completed BIOL6002 Protein Purification: Principles and Practice AND must not have completed BIOTECH7050 BIOTECH3030 (UoA)
courses.aim: This course equips learners with essential skills for purifying biotechnologically significant proteins and understanding how they are adapted to large-scale industrial production. Throughout the course, students will explore a variety of protein purification techniques through interactive workshops and hands-on laboratory practicals. Techniques include affinity chromatography, ion exchange chromatography and gel filtration. Learners will apply their new-found knowledge to the purification of novel proteins of biotechnological interest, discovering how to evaluate the resulting proteins for commercial regulatory requirements. By the end of this course, learners will be well-prepared to contribute to the efficient and compliant production of biotechnologically relevant proteins in commercial settings.

clos.text: Investigate and analyse protein characteristics, recognising their implications for the selection of purification methods and conditions.

courses.aim: The course deals with concepts and theory of geographic information systems and their use for environmental mapping, spatial modelling and analysis. Topics covered include the relationship of GIS models to real-world perception and map representation, vector and raster systems; spatial modelling; translation of problems into GIS procedures; attribute manipulation and recoding, operations including arithmetic and Boolean overlay, reclassification, proximity and neighbourhood analyses; input of data to GIS; database structures; interpolation of surfaces form point and vector data; applications and case studies. courses.aim: This course explores connections between nutrition in early life and its impact on our metabolism, physiology, and healthy ageing. A healthy start to life is critical and nutritional imbalances early in life can increase chronic disease risk. We are living longer, and this comes with an additional set of nutritional challenges. The aim of this course is for students to investigate how early life nutrition impacts future chronic disease risk and how nutrition and metabolism are linked with healthy ageing. Students will also explore how our genetic makeup contributes to healthy ageing and explores the feasibility of personalised nutrition.
